fieldData.excerpt: Public incident report on the Radix Engine vault-authorisation vulnerability and loss of network liveness on 31 August 2026.
fieldData.main-content:
Incident reference: RDX-INC-2026-0831
Incident date: 31 August 2026
Report version: v1.4, 17 September 2026
Status: Contained. Root cause fixed. Network restoration in progress.

1. Executive summary

On 31 August 2026 an attacker exploited a previously undetected vulnerability in the Radix Engine, the execution layer of the Radix network, to withdraw assets from third-party vaults without the owners' authorisation. The stolen assets were routed off the network through the Hyperlane bridge and sold on external chains.

The vulnerability was not a bridge failure, a validator failure or a compromise of any user's private keys. It was a defect in how the Radix Engine enforced ownership of vaults when a vault reference was passed into smart-contract code. That defect was introduced during a code tidy-up carried out in June 2023 by RDX Works Limited, the Foundation's contracted protocol development partner at the time, and was not detected by the subsequent independent security audit conducted by Zellic in August 2024.

Within approximately three hours of the first report, the Foundation, Hyperlane and members of the Radix validator community had shut down the Hyperlane routes and, by taking sufficient validator stake offline, deliberately broken the network's liveness so that no further transaction could be committed. This stopped any further exploitation. A fix to the Radix Engine and accompanying node software has since been written, independently reviewed and tested by audit firms and other trusted security parties. The matter has been reported to the States of Jersey Police and to UK law enforcement, and the Foundation has supplied extensive forensic evidence.

This report sets out what happened, why, how it was contained, how it has been fixed, and what the Foundation is doing to ensure a safe return to normal operation.

2. Background: audit history of the Radix Engine

The Radix Engine is the component of the Radix node that executes transactions and enforces the ownership and access rules for every asset on the network.

  • Pre-June 2023: The Radix Engine was audited by Hacken and passed.
  • June 2023: The RDX Works development team carried out a routine code tidy-up of the Radix Engine. This change introduced the vulnerability described below.
  • August 2024: The Radix protocol, including the engine kernel containing the vulnerability, was audited by Zellic. The protocol passed with a high score for a Layer 1 protocol. The vulnerability was not detected.
  • 31 August 2026: The vulnerability was identified and exploited by an external attacker.

The Foundation's assessment, shared by the external forensic team, is that the attacker used AI-assisted code-analysis tooling to locate the vulnerability in the publicly available Radix Engine source code. The exploit was highly targeted and left a minimal footprint, which is consistent with automated discovery followed by a deliberately engineered attack. The wider industry should expect AI tooling to surface latent defects that conventional audits have missed.

3. The vulnerability

3.1 Plain-language description

Every asset on Radix is held in a vault. A vault can only be withdrawn from by the account or component that owns it. The Radix Engine is responsible for enforcing that rule.

The defect allowed a transaction to name any vault on the network by its internal address, pass that address into a purpose-built piece of smart-contract code, and call the vault's ordinary withdraw function. The engine should have rejected the call because the caller did not own the vault. Because of the defect, the engine treated the reference as if it were a normal, authorised reference and permitted the withdrawal.

3.2 Technical summary

Internal vault addresses supplied in a transaction manifest are classified by the engine as direct-access references, intended only for explicitly direct operations such as recall. When such a reference was passed into a package call frame and the package then invoked ordinary methods (get_amount and take) on the vault, the engine permitted those calls to proceed even though take is not a direct-access method and should not have been callable through a direct-access reference. The visibility check that should have blocked the ordinary method call did not recognise the borrowed direct-access origin of the reference, so the withdrawal proceeded, subject only to the resource's withdrawer role.

The exploit was carried out entirely by the attacker's own package acting on the Radix Engine. The Hyperlane package played no part in the exploit mechanism; it was used purely as the destination to which the withdrawn assets were sent. The affected resources and their role configurations were correct. The engine was not enforcing the ownership boundary those configurations relied upon.

3.3 What was not affected

  • No user, validator or Foundation private keys were compromised.
  • Radix consensus operated correctly throughout, both in including the malicious transactions and later in ceasing to make progress once validator stake was taken offline.
  • The Hyperlane bridge, its validators and its message verification operated correctly. Every release on a destination chain matched a legitimately committed burn on Radix; the theft occurred on Radix before the bridge was used.
  • No admin, recall or clawback badge was used or abused.

4. Incident timeline

All times are UTC on 31 August 2026 unless stated. Local Jersey time (BST) is one hour ahead.

  • 16:02-16:57: The attacker executed 26 exploit transactions on Radix, withdrawing bridged assets from third-party vaults and dispatching them across the Hyperlane bridge to Ethereum, BNB Chain and Solana.
  • 17:37: Community validators and Radix team members identified the unauthorised withdrawals and escalated to Foundation leadership. Incident response began.
  • 17:53-18:09: Hyperlane removed Radix from its validator, relayer and scraper operations; Radix validator infrastructure for the bridge was scaled to zero.
  • 18:09: SEAL 911 was engaged to lead an independent investigation. The Foundation board was briefed.
  • 18:11: Zellic was engaged and began investigation.
  • 18:35: Hyperlane was asked to shut down the remaining Hyperlane routes for Radix assets.
  • 18:46: All Foundation market-making activity on centralised exchanges was stopped; exchanges were asked to pause trading pending investigation.
  • 19:10-19:45: The Foundation completed the multi-signature transaction required to pause the Ethereum route at the bridge level.
  • Approximately 19:30: Initial findings from SEAL 911 and community researchers converged on a bug in the Radix Engine's vault-authorisation logic.
  • 20:30: The Foundation, board members and key validators determined that all network assets were at risk and decided to break network liveness by taking sufficient validator stake offline.
  • 20:30-23:30: Network liveness was broken through coordinated validator action; no further transactions could be committed. Planning for a fix and restoration began.
  • 1 September, 11:00: A candidate Radix Engine fix was presented for review. A plan for independent verification and node software updates was agreed.
  • 2 September, 07:33 and 07:47: Crime reports were submitted to the States of Jersey Police and UK police through Action Fraud.

5. Detection and containment

5.1 Detection

Members of the Radix community operating validator nodes first noticed bridged assets being drained through the Hyperlane bridge. They escalated immediately to the Radix team, which contacted Foundation leadership. The Foundation established within minutes that the bridge itself was functioning correctly and that the problem lay on the Radix side.

5.2 Shutting down the bridge

The Foundation contacted Hyperlane directly. Hyperlane disabled its Radix validator, relayer and scraper operations and coordinated with its independent validator operators to take their Radix signers offline. In parallel, the Foundation executed a multi-signature transaction to pause the routes at contract level. Together these steps ensured that no further Radix-originated bridge messages could be delivered.

5.3 Breaking network liveness

Once the investigation established that the root cause was in the Radix Engine rather than in any single application, it was clear that bridged assets had been targeted simply because they had liquidity on other chains; in principle, any vault on the network was exposed. The Foundation convened an emergency call with key validators and board members and decided to stop the network committing transactions.

The Radix network cannot be paused or switched off by any single party, and it was not halted in that sense. Instead, validator node operators voluntarily and in coordination took sufficient stake offline that the remaining validators could no longer reach the majority of stake that consensus requires. Nodes continued to run and attempt normal operation, but without enough participating stake no further transaction could be committed. Liveness was lost within approximately three hours of the initial report, and from that point no further transaction has been committed.

5.4 Other containment measures

  • All Foundation market making on centralised exchanges was stopped and exchanges were asked to pause XRD deposits, withdrawals and trading.
  • The malicious package, transaction manifests, receipts, affected vault lists and bridge operator logs were preserved for forensic analysis before any clean-up activity.

6. Impact

The attacker withdrew Hyperlane-bridged representations of ETH, WBTC, USDT, USDC, BNB and SOL, together with a small quantity of XRD used to pay transaction fees, from vaults owned by a number of ecosystem packages and accounts, including liquidity pools. The assets that reached destination chains were sold for ETH shortly afterwards. Although the attacker targeted bridged assets for their liquidity on other chains, any package or account holding vaults was at risk.

Because network liveness was broken before the vulnerability could be applied more widely, the Foundation is not aware of unauthorised withdrawals beyond those identified in the timeline above.

7. Remediation

7.1 The fix

A fix to the Radix Engine was developed within 48 hours of the liveness break. The fix enforces the receiver capability before a method call frame is constructed: an ordinary method call on a vault is now rejected when the caller holds only a direct-access reference, while intentional direct-access operations continue to work as designed. Defence-in-depth changes ensure that a direct-access reference retains that classification across borrows and cannot be used as an ordinary receiver by any call path.

Regression tests were added at unit level to prove the classification defect is closed and at integration level to prove that an unauthorised take on a third-party vault, with no intent signers, is rejected. Positive tests confirm that legitimate recall, and normal calls on owned and global objects, are unaffected.

7.2 Node software updates

Applying the fix required a coordinated protocol upgrade of every validator node. Additional engineering was undertaken to restart the network safely from the state at which liveness was lost, ensure all nodes apply the corrected engine at the same state version, and prevent any transaction prepared against the vulnerable engine from executing after restart.

7.3 Independent verification

The Foundation has not relied on its own testing. The fix and updated node software have been reviewed and tested by the audit firms engaged during the incident and by other trusted parties. Trusted security parties have also independently deployed test networks running the patched code and conducted adversarial testing. Their collective conclusion is that, while no software can be guaranteed free of defects, no critical security issues were identified in the patched Radix Engine or node software. The Foundation is satisfied that the network can be safely restored on that basis.

8. Law enforcement

The Foundation has reported the incident as a crime to the States of Jersey Police and to UK police through Action Fraud. Both have been supplied with extensive forensic evidence, including the complete ledger of exploit transactions, malicious package code, attacker-controlled addresses on Radix and each destination chain, the liquidation trail, and a full technical account of the vulnerability and how it was introduced.

The Foundation will continue to cooperate fully with law enforcement and with any exchange or analytics provider tracing the proceeds. Exchanges that receive or have received funds associated with attacker-controlled addresses are asked to contact the Foundation.

9. Root cause analysis and lessons learned

9.1 Root cause

The vulnerability was introduced in June 2023 during a routine code tidy-up of the Radix Engine. Three individually reasonable behaviours in the call-frame reference model combined into an unsafe path. The change was not caught by internal review at the time and was not detected by Zellic's independent audit in August 2024, despite that audit covering the kernel in which the defect sat.

9.2 Lessons

  • Refactoring is a security event. Code tidy-ups and refactors of security-critical components must be treated with the same rigour as new features: separate reviewers, explicit threat modelling of the reference and capability model, and a dedicated regression suite for authorisation boundaries.
  • Audits are necessary but not sufficient. Audits sample; they do not prove. The Foundation recommends supplementing audits with continuous automated analysis, including AI-assisted review of the kind the attacker is believed to have used.
  • External development must be evidenced. Where protocol code is outsourced, the contracting entity must evidence its change-control, review and testing processes, and the Foundation must retain independent verification capability rather than relying on the contractor's assurance.
  • RDX Works Limited. RDX Works Limited were informed of the situation and the root cause and have yet to respond.
  • Coordinated halt capability worked and must be formalised. The network was halted by voluntary validator action within three hours. The Foundation will work with the validator community to document and rehearse this procedure so it can be executed faster and with clearer authority in future.
